title: Does the drift model work on data it has never seen? 2019–2022 estimation, 2023–2024 test, walk-forward

explain.prompt: The trader asks: “The drift model had t-stats of −4.8 in 2019–2022. Does it work?” Answer in 5–7 sentences with your numbers: how the test was set up, in-sample vs out-of-sample errors, the comparison with the baselines, what the walk-forward adds, and what you can and cannot conclude.
rubric: Set-up: target = log WTI return over the 10 trading days after each 14:30 settlement; features = what was known at that settlement (latest published surprise, demand growth as known). The model is estimated on 2019–2022 only, on rows whose 10-day target was realised by 31 Dec 2022 (991 rows), frozen, then applied to 2023–2024 (492 rows). No random split.

In sample: R² 3.0 %, MAE 7.35 %, RMSE 9.69 %. Out of sample: MAE 6.21 %, RMSE 7.85 % — lower than in sample only because 2023–2024 was calmer, which is why errors must be compared with a baseline on the same period.
On the same 2023–2024 rows, predicting zero gives MAE 5.98 % / RMSE 7.56 %, and the training mean 6.06 % / 7.63 %: the model is worse than both baselines; its direction is right 52 % of the time.

Walk-forward (re-estimated at each quarter of 2023–2024 on all rows whose target was known before the origin): MAE 6.17 %, RMSE 7.81 % — still worse than zero; the surprise coefficient shrinks from −0.51 % to −0.38 % per mb as 2023–2024 enters the sample. The relationship was a feature of the training period (concentrated in 2020–2022), not a stable law.

In-sample R² and t-stats measure fit to the past; out-of-sample error against a baseline measures usefulness. A weak out-of-sample result is a valid finding, not a failed test. A good one would not have proved causality or guaranteed profits either.
Purging matters: rows from late December 2022 have targets ending in January 2023 — using them would let test-period prices into the estimation.
